title: Zoonotic Potential of Influenza A Viruses: A Comprehensive Overview

subsections.section_title: Virological Foundations of Influenza A and Determinants of Host Range
subsections.subsection_title: Genome Organization and Viral Proteins
subsections.content:
Influenza A virus is an enveloped orthomyxovirus with a segmented, negative-sense RNA genome comprising eight viral RNA segments that are packaged as ribonucleoprotein complexes (vRNPs) with nucleoprotein (NP) and the heterotrimeric polymerase PB2, PB1, and PA ref [1], ref [2]. This architecture links replication, transcription, and genome packaging to host adaptation, because each segment carries both coding information and cis-acting packaging signals that influence segment compatibility and reassortment potential ref [3]. Virion morphology and assembly are coordinated by matrix protein M1 beneath the lipid envelope and by the ion channel M2, which promotes endosomal uncoating after entry ref [4].

The major surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), determine cell entry and progeny virus release, respectively, and are the principal antigens under immune selection ref [5]. HA mediates receptor binding and low-pH-triggered membrane fusion, whereas NA cleaves sialic acids to prevent virion aggregation and facilitate spread through mucus and infected tissues ref [5], ref [6]. Internal gene products also make major contributions to host range: NP and the polymerase complex govern efficient replication in a species-specific cellular environment, while NS1 antagonizes innate immune responses and the nuclear export protein (NEP/NS2) coordinates vRNP export and influences polymerase function ref [7], ref [8].

Several segments encode additional proteins through splicing, leaky scanning, or alternative reading frames, expanding the functional repertoire of this compact genome. PB1 also encodes PB1-F2 and N40, proteins implicated in virulence and modulation of host responses ref [9], while the PA segment encodes PA-X, a host shutoff factor that dampens cellular gene expression and can alter pathogenicity ref [10]. Thus, the modular influenza A genome couples structural economy with functional plasticity, a central feature underlying viral diversity, interspecies transmission, and pandemic emergence.

subsections.section_title: Virological Foundations of Influenza A and Determinants of Host Range
subsections.subsection_title: Subtype Diversity and Natural Reservoirs
subsections.content:
Influenza A viruses exhibit exceptional subtype diversity, defined by combinations of antigenically distinct hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) proteins. Wild aquatic birds, especially ducks, geese, swans, gulls, and shorebirds, constitute the principal natural reservoir in which most HA and NA subtypes are maintained with extensive genetic diversity and generally limited clinical disease ref [11], ref [12]. Long-term surveillance established that these avian reservoirs support global circulation of multiple subtype constellations and provide the source population from which viruses periodically enter domestic birds and mammals ref [12], ref [13].

Reservoir structure is nevertheless heterogeneous. Dabbling ducks are central for maintenance of many low-pathogenic avian influenza viruses, whereas gulls and shorebirds harbor partly distinct lineages and contribute to intercontinental movement along migratory flyways ref [13], ref [14]. In poultry, onward adaptation and amplification can reshape subtype prevalence, most notably with H5 and H7 viruses that may evolve from low- to highly pathogenic forms after introduction from wild birds ref [15]. Geographic lineage segregation, especially between Eurasian and North American avian gene pools, further structures subtype diversity, although reassortment and bird migration intermittently bridge these divides ref [13], ref [14].

Beyond birds, swine are a major secondary reservoir because they sustain enzootic H1 and H3 lineages derived from avian and human ancestors and facilitate the long-term persistence of reassortant viruses with zoonotic potential ref [16], ref [17]. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic exemplified how complex swine reservoir dynamics can generate globally transmissible viruses from multiple ancestral lineages ref [18]. Other mammals, including horses, dogs, and bats, host more restricted influenza A lineages, expanding the recognized ecological breadth of the virus even if their contribution to sustained human emergence is comparatively limited ref [19], ref [20].

subsections.section_title: Virological Foundations of Influenza A and Determinants of Host Range
subsections.subsection_title: Receptor Binding Specificity and Tissue Tropism
subsections.content:
A central determinant of influenza A host range is the specificity of the hemagglutinin (HA) glycoprotein for terminal sialic acids on host glycoconjugates. Avian-adapted viruses preferentially bind sialic acid linked to galactose by an α2,3 bond, whereas human-adapted strains generally favor α2,6 linkages; this distinction was established by comparative studies of receptor binding and human tracheal tissue tropism ref [21], ref [22]. Structural analyses further showed that relatively small changes in the HA receptor-binding site can switch binding preference, helping explain how zoonotic strains acquire compatibility with human airway receptors ref [23], ref [24].

Receptor distribution along the respiratory tract strongly shapes tissue tropism and transmission potential. Lectin histochemistry and glycan analyses demonstrated that α2,6-linked receptors predominate in the human upper airway, while α2,3-linked glycans are more abundant in the lower respiratory tract, conjunctiva, and in avian intestinal and respiratory epithelia ref [25], ref [26]. This anatomical gradient helps explain why many avian viruses can infect humans but replicate mainly in the lower lung, causing severe disease without efficient onward spread. In ferrets and ex vivo human airway models, acquisition of human-like receptor binding correlates with enhanced upper-airway replication and transmissibility, although receptor binding alone is not sufficient ref [27], ref [28].

Importantly, receptor specificity is more nuanced than a simple α2,3/α2,6 dichotomy. Glycan topology, chain length, fucosylation, sulfation, and multivalent avidity all influence productive attachment, and contemporary glycan microarray studies show that different HA subtypes recognize distinct subsets of glycans within the same linkage class ref [29], ref [30]. Thus, tissue tropism and host range emerge from the interaction between HA binding phenotype, neuraminidase balance, and the spatial organization of compatible glycans in target tissues.

subsections.section_title: Virological Foundations of Influenza A and Determinants of Host Range
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Reassortment, Mutation, and Viral Evolution
subsections.content:
Influenza A virus evolution is driven by the interplay of mutation and segment exchange. Because the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is error-prone and lacks proofreading, antigenic drift continuously generates amino-acid variation that can alter receptor binding, antigenicity, replication efficiency, and host range ref [31]. At the population scale, this process produces rapid lineage turnover under immune and ecological selection, as shown by phylodynamic analyses of human influenza A/H3N2 ref [32].

The segmented genome additionally enables reassortment when distinct viruses coinfect the same cell, allowing whole gene segments to be exchanged and thereby creating genotypes with large phenotypic jumps. Experimental work demonstrated that reassortment among human H3N2 strains can proceed frequently, although gene constellations are constrained by segment mismatch and epistatic incompatibilities ref [33], ref [34]. In nature, reassortment has repeatedly generated viruses of public-health concern, including the triple-reassortant swine viruses that contributed internal genes to later zoonotic strains ref [35] and the 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus, whose ancestry linked North American and Eurasian swine lineages ref [18].

Long-term viral evolution therefore reflects both opportunity and constraint. Global analyses show that host switching and sustained emergence depend not only on mutation supply but also on compatibility among polymerase, surface, and packaging functions across segments ref [36]. The broad avian gene pool, especially in wild birds, provides a major reservoir of reassortment diversity from which lineages can seed domestic poultry, swine, and occasionally humans ref [37], while adaptation after cross-species transmission may proceed through parallel or convergent substitutions that stabilize replication in the new host ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Virological Foundations of Influenza A and Determinants of Host Range
subsections.subsection_title: Molecular Markers of Mammalian Adaptation
subsections.content:
Mammalian adaptation in influenza A virus is a polygenic trait shaped by mutations that improve replication at lower temperatures, optimize use of mammalian host factors, and alter innate immune antagonism. Among the best-established markers are substitutions in the polymerase complex, especially PB2 E627K and D701N, which enhance viral replication and virulence in mammals by increasing polymerase activity and facilitating nuclear import in mammalian cells ref [39], ref [40]. Adaptive changes can also arise through PB2 590/591 residues that compensate for the absence of 627K in some pandemic-lineage viruses ref [41].

Additional determinants occur across multiple segments. In avian-origin H5N1 and related viruses, PB1-F2 N66S has been linked to increased pathogenicity in mammals, while changes in NP and polymerase acidic protein can further tune replication efficiency in mammalian hosts ref [42], ref [43]. At the surface glycoprotein level, mammalian adaptation often coincides with hemagglutinin mutations that shift binding from avian-type alpha2,3-linked to human-type alpha2,6-linked sialic acids, a prerequisite for efficient upper-respiratory transmission; classic examples include H2 and H3 pandemic-associated receptor-binding changes and key H5 mutations identified experimentally ref [44], ref [28].

Adaptation also involves balancing entry and release functions and evading host restriction. Neuraminidase stalk alterations, M-segment changes, and NS1 mutations can modulate replication, transmission, and interferon antagonism in mammals ref [45], ref [46]. Importantly, no single substitution is universally predictive: mammalian adaptation reflects epistatic interactions among polymerase, HA, NA, and host background, as illustrated by comparative analyses of avian and zoonotic influenza viruses and by gain-of-function studies on airborne transmission in ferrets ref [28], ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Ecological and Epidemiological Interfaces of Zoonotic Emergence
subsections.subsection_title: Wild Bird Reservoirs and Viral Maintenance
subsections.content:
Wild aquatic birds, especially Anseriformes and Charadriiformes, constitute the principal natural reservoir of influenza A viruses, harboring extensive subtype diversity with generally low clinical impact and thereby enabling long-term viral persistence ref [48], ref [13]. Surveillance and phylogenetic analyses show that nearly all hemagglutinin and neuraminidase subtypes circulate in these hosts, where infections are often concentrated in the intestinal tract and shed into aquatic environments, facilitating fecal–oral transmission within migratory populations ref [48], ref [49].

Viral maintenance in wild birds is shaped by host demography, migration, and environmental persistence. Juvenile recruitment after breeding seasons increases the pool of immunologically naive hosts, helping to generate predictable seasonal peaks in prevalence, particularly in dabbling ducks ref [50], ref [51]. Water can function as a transient environmental reservoir because low temperature, neutral pH, and low salinity prolong infectivity, creating opportunities for indirect transmission at shared wetlands ref [52]. At broader scales, intercontinental flyways support gene flow and reassortment, although movement is structured enough to produce recognizable Eurasian and American lineage patterns ref [53], ref [54].

These reservoir dynamics are epidemiologically consequential because wild birds intermittently introduce viruses into domestic poultry and occasionally seed highly pathogenic lineages after adaptation in gallinaceous hosts ref [55], ref [15]. Thus, wild bird systems should be understood not simply as static reservoirs, but as dynamic ecological networks in which host movement, environmental survival, and viral evolution jointly govern zoonotic emergence risk.

subsections.section_title: Ecological and Epidemiological Interfaces of Zoonotic Emergence
subsections.subsection_title: Swine as Mixing Vessels and Amplifying Hosts
subsections.content:
Swine occupy a pivotal position at the animal–human interface because their respiratory tract supports infection by both avian- and human-adapted influenza A viruses, creating opportunities for reassortment and onward spread. The long-recognized concern that pigs can serve as “mixing vessels” arose from evidence that their tracheal epithelium expresses both α2,3- and α2,6-linked sialic acid receptors, although receptor distribution is heterogeneous across the swine respiratory tract and does not by itself determine host range ref [22], ref [56]. Experimental studies further show that pigs are susceptible to diverse avian, human, and swine influenza lineages, enabling coinfection under field conditions ref [57].

The epidemiological importance of swine is illustrated by repeated interspecies transmission and viral diversification in pig populations. Human seasonal viruses have entered swine repeatedly, establishing lineages that later reassorted with endemic swine viruses; conversely, avian-origin gene segments have also become incorporated into swine influenza gene constellations ref [58], ref [59]. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic was the clearest demonstration of this process, with a virus generated from multiple swine lineages in North America and Eurasia before successful emergence in humans ref [18], ref [60]. Once introduced, dense production systems, animal movement, and age-structured herd immunity can facilitate amplification and persistence of reassortant viruses within swine populations ref [61].

These dynamics make swine both a reservoir of genetic novelty and a source of zoonotic exposure. Occupational studies have repeatedly found elevated serologic evidence of swine influenza infection among farmers, veterinarians, and abattoir workers, supporting bidirectional transmission at the human–swine interface ref [62], ref [63]. Accordingly, surveillance in pigs is not only an agricultural priority but a core component of pandemic preparedness, particularly where industrial production, live animal trade, and close human contact increase opportunities for spillover.

subsections.section_title: Ecological and Epidemiological Interfaces of Zoonotic Emergence
subsections.subsection_title: Poultry Production Systems and Live Animal Markets
subsections.content:
Poultry production systems create epidemiological settings that can sustain avian influenza A virus circulation and increase opportunities for zoonotic exposure. High host density, rapid flock turnover, and spatial clustering of farms facilitate transmission within and between holdings, while species mixing across chickens, ducks, geese, and quail broadens the range of susceptible hosts and viral genotypes. In southern China and neighboring regions, domestic ducks in particular have been implicated as important maintenance hosts linking wild-waterfowl viruses to terrestrial poultry production systems ref [64], ref [65]. The establishment and spread of H5N1 in domestic birds illustrated how trade networks and intensive production can transform localized infection into persistent regional epizootics ref [66].

Live bird markets amplify these risks by concentrating birds from multiple sources, permitting prolonged viral persistence through continual replenishment, overnight holding, and environmental contamination. Longitudinal surveillance in Hong Kong demonstrated that market systems can maintain and disseminate influenza viruses and that interventions such as monthly rest days and bans on overnight poultry holding reduce viral isolation rates ref [67], ref [68]. Market exposure was a central feature of human H7N9 emergence in China, with epidemiological analyses linking many early human cases to visits to live poultry markets and showing that market closure was associated with marked declines in incidence ref [69], ref [70]. Viral ecology in these markets is further shaped by interspecies contact and reassortment among co-circulating avian strains, helping generate genotypes with altered host range or zoonotic potential ref [59], ref [71].

These observations underscore that spillover risk is not simply a function of virus presence in poultry, but of how production and retail systems structure contact among birds, workers, traders, and consumers. Accordingly, biosecurity along the supply chain, market rest and cleaning policies, separation of aquatic and terrestrial poultry, and transitions away from high-risk retail configurations remain central tools for reducing zoonotic emergence at the poultry–human interface ref [68], ref [70], ref [72].

subsections.section_title: Ecological and Epidemiological Interfaces of Zoonotic Emergence
subsections.subsection_title: Occupational and Environmental Exposure Pathways
subsections.content:
Occupational exposure is among the clearest interfaces for zoonotic influenza transmission because it generates repeated, high-intensity contact with infected animals, secretions, and contaminated fomites. Elevated seroreactivity to swine influenza viruses has been documented in swine-exposed workers, supporting frequent subclinical or mild infections at the human–swine interface ref [73]. Analogously, poultry cullers, farm workers, and live-poultry market personnel have experienced direct infection during avian influenza outbreaks, including H5N1 and H7N7 episodes, demonstrating that handling, slaughtering, defeathering, and carcass disposal can all serve as transmission opportunities ref [74], ref [75], ref [76].

Environmental pathways extend risk beyond direct animal handling. Influenza A viruses can persist for meaningful periods in water, feces, and on surfaces under favorable temperature and salinity conditions, creating opportunities for indirect exposure in farms, transport equipment, and market environments ref [77]. Viable avian influenza virus and viral RNA have been detected in aerosols and environmental samples from live-animal markets and infected poultry settings, indicating that inhalation of contaminated dust or droplets may contribute to spillover risk ref [78], ref [79]. Such pathways help explain why market closure, rest days, and decontamination reduce both environmental contamination and human infection incidence in affected settings ref [80].

Risk is further shaped by biosecurity, household proximity to livestock, and personal protective practices. Case-control studies of human H5N1 infection have consistently linked disease to direct or nearby exposure to sick or dead poultry, especially where backyard production, home slaughter, and limited infection control blur the boundary between occupational and domestic environments ref [81], ref [82]. Accordingly, zoonotic emergence is best understood not as a single contact event but as the cumulative result of repeated occupational and environmental encounters across production, marketing, and household spaces.

subsections.section_title: Ecological and Epidemiological Interfaces of Zoonotic Emergence
subsections.subsection_title: Geographic, Seasonal, and Socioeconomic Drivers
subsections.content:
Geographic variation in zoonotic influenza risk reflects the overlap of reservoir ecology, animal production intensity, and human population density. In East and Southeast Asia, river-delta agroecosystems and dense poultry and swine production have repeatedly been associated with the emergence and persistence of avian-origin influenza viruses, including H5N1 and H7N9, while migratory flyways connect these local systems to broader viral dispersal networks ref [83], ref [13], ref [84]. Spatial analyses of H7N9 further showed that risk clustered where live-poultry market density, poultry movement, and human settlement coincided, underscoring the importance of geographic interfaces rather than reservoir presence alone ref [85], ref [86].

Seasonality modifies these interfaces by shaping host aggregation, virus survival, and human contact patterns. In temperate regions, influenza transmission often peaks in cooler, drier months, conditions that can increase viral stability and susceptibility in hosts, whereas in tropical settings seasonality is more heterogeneous and may track rainfall, market cycles, or migratory bird movements ref [87], ref [88]. For avian influenza specifically, winter migration and overwintering of wild birds can reseed poultry systems, while festival-related surges in poultry trade may transiently amplify exposure opportunities ref [13], ref [85].

Socioeconomic conditions mediate how geographic and seasonal pressures translate into spillover. Informal marketing chains, limited biosecurity, smallholder dependence on mixed-species farming, and constrained access to veterinary compensation can discourage reporting and sustain circulation at the human-animal interface ref [89], ref [90]. At the same time, rapid urbanization and rising demand for animal protein intensify movement of birds, pigs, and people across regions, creating connected risk landscapes in which local outbreaks can more readily generate zoonotic exposure and wider dissemination ref [84], ref [91].

subsections.section_title: Mechanisms and Barriers of Cross-Species Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Species Barrier Concepts in Influenza Ecology
subsections.content:
In influenza ecology, the species barrier is best viewed as a multilevel filter rather than a single molecular incompatibility. Aquatic birds constitute the major reservoir of influenza A virus diversity, but successful host jumps depend on ecological contact, exposure dose, tissue tropism, and the capacity of viral gene constellations to function in a new host background ref [92], ref [93]. Cross-species transmission is therefore shaped jointly by host community structure and by viral traits that determine whether spillover events remain dead ends or generate onward transmission chains ref [94], ref [95].

A key conceptual advance has been recognition that influenza viruses circulate in partially connected host pools. Wild birds maintain broad subtype diversity, whereas domestic poultry, swine, horses, dogs, and humans represent secondary ecological niches with distinct selection pressures ref [92], ref [96]. Swine are especially important at the animal-human interface because they are infected by avian and human-lineage viruses and can support reassortment, creating genotypes with altered host range and transmission properties ref [97], ref [98]. Historical analyses of the 1957, 1968, and 2009 pandemics underscore that emergence often reflects ecological opportunity coupled to reassortment and adaptive tuning rather than direct linear descent from a single reservoir lineage ref [98], ref [99].

Accordingly, species barriers in influenza should be framed as dynamic and context dependent. Host phylogeny matters, but agricultural intensification, live-animal marketing, farming practices, and repeated human exposure can lower ecological barriers and increase the frequency of transient infections from which adaptive variants may be selected ref [94], ref [95], ref [100]. This ecological perspective helps explain why only a small minority of zoonotic infections progress from spillover to sustained human transmission ref [99], ref [101].

subsections.section_title: Mechanisms and Barriers of Cross-Species Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Viral Entry, Replication, and Host Compatibility
subsections.content:
Cross-species infection begins with compatibility between the viral hemagglutinin (HA) and host-cell sialylated receptors, but this barrier is shaped by both glycan topology and tissue distribution. Avian-adapted viruses typically prefer terminal Neu5Ac\alpha2,3-linked glycans, whereas human-adapted viruses preferentially bind Neu5Ac\alpha2,6-linked glycans, a distinction classically linked to host range and airway tropism ref [22], ref [102]. Human upper airways are enriched for \alpha2,6-linked receptors, while \alpha2,3-linked glycans are more prominent in the lower respiratory tract, helping explain why many avian viruses can infect humans sporadically yet transmit poorly ref [103].

Entry alone is insufficient: productive replication requires viral polymerase activity in the new cellular environment. Amino-acid changes in PB2, especially E627K and D701N, enhance replication of avian-origin viruses in mammalian cells and are recurrent markers of mammalian adaptation ref [104], ref [105]. More broadly, species-specific dependence on host cofactors constrains ribonucleoprotein function; ANP32 proteins are now recognized as key determinants of polymerase compatibility, with differences between avian and mammalian ANP32 family members helping define host restriction and adaptation trajectories ref [106], ref [107].

Post-entry compatibility is further influenced by HA acid stability and the functional balance between HA receptor binding and neuraminidase cleavage, which together shape fusion, release, and transmissibility. Human-adapted viruses generally exhibit greater HA stability in the mildly acidic environment of the respiratory tract, whereas many zoonotic avian viruses retain less stable HAs that may favor replication in birds but reduce airborne fitness in mammals ref [108], ref [109]. Experimental work with ferrets has shown that efficient transmission emerges only when receptor specificity, polymerase competence, and HA stability are jointly optimized, underscoring that host switching is a multigenic phenotype rather than a single-mutation event ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Mechanisms and Barriers of Cross-Species Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Innate and Adaptive Immune Pressures
subsections.content:
After spillover, influenza A viruses encounter potent innate defenses that often determine whether infection remains abortive or progresses. Pattern-recognition pathways centered on RIG-I and type I/III interferons restrict replication, while species-specific host factors can sharply reduce polymerase activity in a new host. A central example is the human MxA restriction system, which suppresses many avian-origin viruses unless they acquire compensatory nucleoprotein changes; this creates a major evolutionary hurdle during adaptation to humans ref [110], ref [111]. Interferon-stimulated transmembrane proteins also limit entry and fusion, adding another layer of early inhibition at mucosal sites ref [112].

Successful cross-species variants frequently encode antagonists of innate immunity. The multifunctional NS1 protein blocks interferon induction and host gene expression, and differences in NS1 activity contribute to host range and virulence ref [8]. PB1-F2 can further modulate inflammatory responses and pathogenesis, although its effects vary by strain background ref [113]. More broadly, mammalian adaptation of the polymerase complex helps viruses overcome intracellular restriction and replicate efficiently despite antiviral signaling, linking innate immune evasion to replication fitness ref [114].

Adaptive immunity shapes both spillover risk and onward transmission. Preexisting human antibodies to conserved HA stem epitopes and neuraminidase can partially blunt disease from antigenically novel zoonotic strains, but population immunity is often weak when HA head epitopes are highly divergent ref [115], ref [116]. T-cell cross-reactivity to conserved internal proteins may also mitigate severity without preventing infection, thereby influencing selection after emergence ref [117]. At the population level, immune history can bias susceptibility across age cohorts, as illustrated by H5N1 and H7N9 patterns consistent with HA-group imprinting ref [118].

Together, innate restriction and heterogeneous adaptive immunity create a multilayered filter: zoonotic viruses must evade immediate intracellular defenses, replicate despite species-specific antiviral factors, and then transmit in hosts whose prior immune experience may reduce shedding or disease even in the absence of sterilizing immunity.

subsections.section_title: Mechanisms and Barriers of Cross-Species Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Transmission Modes and Efficiency
subsections.content:
For influenza A viruses, transmission efficiency reflects the combined success of shedding from the donor, environmental survival, deposition at susceptible sites in the recipient, and productive infection after exposure. Experimental work has shown that contact and short-range respiratory transmission dominate in mammals, but their efficiency varies sharply by host species and viral genotype. In ferrets, human-adapted and some reassortant viruses transmit readily by respiratory droplets or aerosols, whereas many purely avian viruses infect inoculated animals yet fail to spread onward, illustrating that spillover competence and transmission competence are separable phenotypes ref [119], ref [27].

Particle size, route of exposure, and stability in air or on surfaces further shape between-host spread. Influenza virus can remain infectious in aerosols, with transmission favored by cool, dry conditions in standard guinea pig and ferret models ref [120], ref [121]. In birds, fecal-oral and waterborne transmission are especially important for avian-adapted viruses, linking host ecology to maintenance and interspecies exposure opportunities ref [122]. By contrast, in humans and other mammals, efficient upper-airway replication and release in exhaled particles are more predictive of sustained spread than systemic virulence alone ref [123], ref [124].

Accordingly, mutations that alter HA stability, receptor-binding balance, neuraminidase activity, or polymerase-supported replication in the upper respiratory tract can markedly change transmissibility. A small set of adaptive changes enabled airborne transmission of H5N1 viruses in ferrets, underscoring how transmission is a multigenic trait constrained by trade-offs between host range, within-host fitness, and environmental persistence ref [28], ref [125]. Quantitative synthesis across animal studies also indicates that inoculation route and dose can strongly bias apparent transmission phenotypes, complicating direct extrapolation to natural animal-human interfaces ref [126].

subsections.section_title: Mechanisms and Barriers of Cross-Species Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: From Spillover to Sustained Human Transmission
subsections.content:
Spillover of influenza A virus into humans is relatively frequent at the animal–human interface, but sustained human transmission is rare because successful emergence requires the joint optimization of receptor use, polymerase activity, immune evasion, and transmissibility. Experimental and epidemiologic analyses of past pandemics indicate that adaptation from avian-like binding toward efficient recognition of human upper-airway glycans is a recurrent prerequisite, yet receptor switching alone is insufficient without compatibility in replication and release in human airway tissues ref [22], ref [127], ref [128].

Work on H5N1 and H7N9 has clarified this multistep transition. In ferret models, only particular constellations of HA mutations that alter receptor specificity and stability, together with changes affecting other gene segments, permit respiratory-droplet spread, underscoring the narrow evolutionary path to airborne transmission ref [28], ref [129]. For avian-origin viruses infecting humans, polymerase adaptations such as PB2 E627K or D701N can enhance replication in mammalian cells and increase virulence, but these changes still do not reliably confer efficient onward spread without additional compensatory traits ref [130], ref [131].

Pandemic emergence also depends on ecological opportunity and stochastic amplification. The 2009 H1N1 virus illustrates how reassortment in swine can assemble a genotype already permissive for human-to-human transmission before detection in people ref [18]. By contrast, repeated zoonotic infections with H5N1 and H7N9 have produced severe disease but little sustained spread, emphasizing that spillover severity and epidemic fitness are distinct properties ref [69], ref [132].

subsections.section_title: Historical and Contemporary Zoonotic Influenza A Events
subsections.subsection_title: Avian-Origin Human Infections
subsections.content:
Avian-origin influenza A infections in humans have been dominated by repeated spillover from poultry-associated viruses, especially H5, H7, and H9 lineages. The 1997 Hong Kong H5N1 outbreak established the modern template for concern: direct transmission from infected birds caused severe human disease and high mortality, while rapid control in live-bird markets curtailed wider spread ref [133]. Subsequent epizootic expansion of highly pathogenic H5N1 across Asia, Europe, and Africa increased opportunities for zoonotic infection, with viral evolution in poultry repeatedly generating genetically and antigenically novel threats ref [134], ref [135].

A second major wave of concern emerged with H7N9 in China from 2013, notable for low pathogenicity in birds but severe pneumonia in humans and strong epidemiological links to live poultry markets ref [69], ref [136]. H7N9 illustrated how cryptic circulation in market systems can delay detection while enabling repeated human exposure. Human infections with H5N6 and H9N2 further underscored that both highly pathogenic and apparently low-pathogenic avian viruses can cross the species barrier; H9N2 is especially important because it contributes internal genes to reassortant zoonotic viruses and is enzootic across poultry in Asia and the Middle East ref [137], ref [138].

Across these events, sustained human-to-human transmission has remained limited, but clusters and molecular studies show partial adaptation to mammalian hosts, including receptor-binding changes and polymerase mutations associated with replication in humans ref [139], ref [140]. Overall, avian-origin human infections recur where dense poultry production, live-bird marketing, and viral genetic diversity coincide, making integrated animal-human surveillance central to preparedness ref [141].

subsections.section_title: Historical and Contemporary Zoonotic Influenza A Events
subsections.subsection_title: Swine-Origin Influenza and Pandemic Emergence
subsections.content:
Swine occupy a pivotal position in influenza A ecology because they are susceptible to avian- and human-adapted viruses as well as established swine lineages, enabling reassortment across host boundaries. This “mixing vessel” role was recognized experimentally decades before the 2009 pandemic and remains central to explanations of pandemic emergence risk in pig populations ref [142], ref [143]. Subsequent global analyses showed that contemporary swine influenza diversity is maintained by repeated bidirectional transmission between humans and pigs, followed by reassortment and local enzootic persistence, creating a large and dynamic gene pool with zoonotic potential ref [144], ref [145].

The 2009 H1N1 pandemic provided the clearest example of swine-origin emergence in humans. Early epidemiological investigations documented sustained human transmission after detection of a novel H1N1 virus in North America ref [146], while genomic analyses traced the virus to multiple reassortment events involving North American and Eurasian swine lineages, highlighting years of undetected evolution in pigs before spillover ref [18], ref [60]. Reviews of the pandemic emphasized that the key failure was not a lack of virulence markers but inadequate surveillance at the human-animal interface, especially in commercial and regional swine systems where reassortant viruses circulated cryptically ref [147].

Post-2009 experience further showed that pandemic emergence is not unique to one lineage. Variant infections such as H3N2v in North America arose from swine viruses carrying the human-origin M gene from the 2009 pandemic strain, illustrating how reverse zoonosis can seed new zoonotic threats in pigs ref [148]. Parallel genomic studies indicate that swine are a long-term reservoir of antigenically diverse viruses with uneven geographic surveillance, reinforcing the need for integrated animal, occupational, and human influenza surveillance to detect lineages with transmission potential before broad community spread occurs ref [145], ref [149].

subsections.section_title: Historical and Contemporary Zoonotic Influenza A Events
subsections.subsection_title: Patterns of Severity, Transmission, and Case Distribution
subsections.content:
Across zoonotic influenza A events, severity and spread are shaped by a recurring mismatch between efficient animal-to-human exposure and poor onward human transmission. For avian-origin viruses such as H5N1 and H7N9, most confirmed cases have followed intense contact with infected poultry or contaminated live-bird market environments, while sustained community transmission has remained rare despite repeated spillover [1,2]. Epidemiologic analyses of H5N1 clusters and H7N9 family clusters found that limited, non-sustained person-to-person transmission can occur, but the effective reproductive number generally remains below the threshold for epidemic spread [3,4].

Case distribution is also highly uneven by age, setting, and surveillance intensity. H5N1 human infections have often been detected in children and young adults and are associated with very high reported case fatality, though ascertainment bias likely enriches severe presentations [1,5]. By contrast, H7N9 cases in China were concentrated in older adults, especially men with poultry-market exposure, and severity estimates evolved as surveillance expanded from severe pneumonia toward milder laboratory-confirmed disease [2,6]. Spatial incidence has repeatedly tracked poultry density, market networks, and seasonality, underscoring the role of agro-ecological context in shaping apparent risk [7].

Swine-origin infections show a different pattern: variant H3N2 and related swine influenza infections are often linked to agricultural fairs and generate sporadic pediatric cases with limited secondary transmission, whereas the 2009 H1N1 pandemic demonstrated that once a virus acquires efficient human transmissibility, severity shifts toward a broader denominator with comparatively lower case fatality but substantial population burden [8,9]. Clinical outcomes in severe and fatal zoonotic cases often correlate with delayed antiviral treatment, viral pneumonia, and hypercytokinemia, indicating that both viral adaptation and host inflammatory responses contribute to disease heterogeneity [10].

Taken together, past outbreaks suggest that crude case fatality ratios, cluster size, and age distribution must be interpreted jointly with exposure setting and surveillance design. Apparent severity may decline as testing broadens, whereas changes in cluster frequency or geographic dispersion may provide earlier warning of altered transmissibility than mortality alone.

subsections.section_title: Historical and Contemporary Zoonotic Influenza A Events
subsections.subsection_title: Genomic and Epidemiological Lessons from Past Outbreaks
subsections.content:
Past zoonotic influenza A outbreaks show that emergence is typically a multi-step process in which reassortment, adaptive mutation, and ecological opportunity interact. Whole-genome analyses of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic established that sustained human transmission can arise from prolonged cryptic evolution in swine followed by reassortment among geographically distinct lineages, underscoring major surveillance gaps at the animal-human interface ref [18]. Retrospective reconstruction of H7N9 similarly showed repeated generation of zoonotic genotypes within Chinese poultry systems, with internal genes supplied by enzootic H9N2 viruses and continued diversification during successive epidemic waves ref [158], ref [69].

Genomic studies also clarified that mammalian adaptation is informative but not deterministic. Experimental and comparative work identified receptor-binding changes and polymerase markers, including PB2 adaptations, that can enhance replication or transmission in mammals, yet field observations show that these features must be interpreted in genomic context rather than as simple predictors of pandemicity ref [159], ref [28]. During H5N1 and H7N9 outbreaks, integration of sequence data with case investigations revealed frequent poultry exposure, limited onward transmission, and occasional family clusters, patterns more consistent with repeated spillover than sustained community spread ref [26], ref [160].

A broader epidemiological lesson is that control depends on linking genomics to exposure networks and real-time risk assessment. Phylodynamic and antigenic analyses of H5Nx spread demonstrated rapid long-distance dissemination through wild birds and poultry trade, while formal risk-assessment frameworks emphasized that changes in host range, geographic spread, and genetic composition must be interpreted together ref [161], ref [162], ref [163]. Collectively, past outbreaks argue for continuous sequencing in animal reservoirs, paired animal-human surveillance, and rapid sharing of metadata sufficient to connect viral evolution with transmission opportunity.

subsections.section_title: Historical and Contemporary Zoonotic Influenza A Events
subsections.subsection_title: Regional Case Studies and Endemic Risk Settings
subsections.content:
Regional case studies show that zoonotic influenza risk is concentrated where dense animal production, live marketing, and close human–animal contact persist. In southern China and Hong Kong, live poultry market systems repeatedly amplified avian influenza exposure, with environmental contamination and poultry movement sustaining human risk; interventions such as market rest days, overnight depopulation, and temporary closures reduced viral detection and incidence, illustrating how endemic risk is structured by market ecology rather than isolated spillover events [1,2]. The emergence of H7N9 further demonstrated that apparently low-pathogenic poultry viruses can generate substantial human disease when embedded in these trading networks [3].

Egypt provides a contrasting endemic setting in which H5N1 became entrenched in backyard and commercial poultry, generating one of the largest national burdens of human avian influenza. Epidemiological analyses linked many infections to household poultry exposure, while viral evolution under endemic circulation complicated control and maintained zoonotic pressure [4,5]. In Southeast Asia, Indonesia and neighboring countries highlighted the role of smallholder poultry systems, informal value chains, and uneven veterinary capacity in sustaining H5N1 circulation and localized human risk [6].

For swine-origin threats, case studies from agricultural fairs in the United States showed how temporary animal aggregation and youth-exhibitor contact facilitated variant H3N2 transmission to humans, emphasizing that endemic risk can emerge in seasonal, event-based interfaces rather than permanent farms alone [7]. At the same time, the 2009 H1N1 pandemic underscored Mexico and North American swine production networks as important ecological settings for reassortment and undetected spread before recognition [8]. More broadly, global analyses identify hotspots where poultry or swine intensification, market connectivity, and limited biosecurity coincide, suggesting that surveillance should prioritize persistent human–animal interfaces rather than only outbreak response [9].

subsections.section_title: Surveillance, Risk Assessment, and Predictive Frameworks
subsections.subsection_title: Integrated One Health Surveillance Systems
subsections.content:
Integrated One Health surveillance for influenza A viruses links animal, human, and environmental data streams to detect emergence before widespread transmission. Experience from highly pathogenic avian influenza has shown that fragmented sectoral surveillance can miss cross-species transmission opportunities, whereas coordinated systems improve situational awareness across wild birds, poultry, swine, and exposed human populations ref [100], ref [170]. Global architectures such as WHO’s GISRS and the OFFLU network illustrate how laboratory sharing, epidemiologic reporting, and veterinary-human health coordination can support early warning and candidate vaccine preparedness ref [171], ref [172].

Operationally, effective systems combine event-based reporting, targeted sampling in high-risk interfaces, and genomic characterization of viruses collected from animals and humans. Risk is concentrated at interfaces shaped by poultry value chains, live bird markets, swine production networks, and migratory bird flyways; surveillance that samples these interfaces has repeatedly identified reassortant and zoonotic lineages before or during human spillover events ref [18], ref [173], ref [174]. Environmental sampling, including market and farm contamination monitoring, can complement host-based surveillance where infection is transient or under-ascertained ref [175].

A central challenge is uneven capacity: countries with the greatest animal-human interface intensity may have limited diagnostic infrastructure, inconsistent metadata collection, and weak integration between veterinary and public health agencies. Practical One Health systems therefore require standardized sampling protocols, interoperable databases, rapid sequence sharing, and governance mechanisms that sustain cross-sector collaboration rather than outbreak-only responses ref [170], ref [172], ref [176], ref [177].

subsections.section_title: Surveillance, Risk Assessment, and Predictive Frameworks
subsections.subsection_title: Genomic Surveillance and Molecular Epidemiology
subsections.content:
Genomic surveillance has become central to zoonotic influenza risk assessment because whole-genome sequencing links viral detection to inferences about origin, reassortment, host adaptation, and geographic spread. Early phylogeographic analyses demonstrated that avian influenza lineages can move over continental scales through poultry trade and wild-bird migration, while also diversifying locally after introduction ref [178], ref [179]. Large-scale sequencing further showed that the segmented genome of influenza A enables frequent reassortment, generating genotypes with altered host range and pathogenicity that would be missed by subtype-based surveillance alone ref [59].

At the molecular level, comparative genomics has identified markers associated with mammalian adaptation and virulence, including polymerase changes such as PB2 E627K and D701N, receptor-binding shifts in hemagglutinin, and polybasic cleavage sites in H5 and H7 viruses ref [180], ref [102]. Genomic analyses of emergent zoonotic viruses have been especially informative for H7N9 and clade 2.3.4.4 H5Nx viruses, revealing repeated reassortment with enzootic poultry viruses, cryptic circulation before human detection, and rapid dissemination across regions and host species ref [181], ref [182], ref [183].

Molecular epidemiology is most informative when sequence data are integrated with metadata on host, production system, location, and sampling intensity. Bayesian phylodynamic approaches can reconstruct introduction histories and transmission corridors, but inference remains sensitive to sparse sampling and uneven sharing of sequences and associated epidemiological data ref [179], ref [184]. Accordingly, genomic surveillance is strongest when embedded in standardized, real-time One Health systems that combine sequence-based monitoring with antigenic characterization and risk assessment frameworks ref [162].

subsections.section_title: Surveillance, Risk Assessment, and Predictive Frameworks
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models for Zoonotic Risk Evaluation
subsections.content:
Experimental systems are central to zoonotic risk evaluation because surveillance data alone rarely reveal whether an animal-origin influenza A virus can replicate efficiently in human tissues, evade existing immunity, or transmit between mammals. Ferret models remain the benchmark for assessing respiratory droplet transmission and pathogenesis, and comparative work has shown clear differences in transmissibility among avian, swine, and human-adapted viruses ref [119], ref [185]. Guinea pigs and, more recently, human airway organoid and ex vivo respiratory explant models provide complementary platforms for quantifying replication competence and tissue tropism under conditions that are not fully captured by sequence-based inference alone ref [186], ref [187].

A major strength of experimental models is their ability to test mechanistic determinants of host adaptation. Classic gain- and loss-of-function studies identified polymerase mutations such as PB2 E627K as important for efficient replication in mammals ref [188], while receptor-binding studies linked shifts in hemagglutinin specificity from avian-type to human-type sialylated glycans with enhanced airborne transmission potential ref [189]. Reverse-genetics experiments with H5N1 further demonstrated that only a limited set of changes can markedly alter transmissibility in ferrets, underscoring both the value and biosafety sensitivity of these approaches ref [28], ref [190].

These models are increasingly integrated into formal risk frameworks. The CDC Influenza Risk Assessment Tool and related approaches explicitly consider mammalian infection, transmission, and pathogenicity data generated in vivo and in vitro when prioritizing viruses for preparedness action ref [191], ref [192]. Nonetheless, model outputs must be interpreted cautiously: no single system fully recapitulates heterogeneous human exposure, immunity, or comorbidity, and inter-laboratory variation, inoculation route, and viral stock preparation can materially influence inferred zoonotic risk.

subsections.section_title: Surveillance, Risk Assessment, and Predictive Frameworks
subsections.subsection_title: Seroepidemiology and Human Exposure Assessment
subsections.content:
Seroepidemiology provides a critical complement to virologic surveillance by identifying prior zoonotic Influenza A virus infections that were mild, subclinical, or missed by routine case finding. Household and occupational studies repeatedly show that infection risk is concentrated in people with frequent poultry or swine contact, but that serologic inference is complicated by antibody cross-reactivity, assay heterogeneity, and uncertain correlates of protection. Reviews of human infection with avian viruses and field studies among exposed workers have therefore emphasized the need to interpret low-titer responses cautiously and in relation to exposure history, local virus ecology, and vaccination background [1,2].

Among avian viruses, H5, H7, and H9 serosurveys have revealed a broader spectrum of human exposure than is apparent from severe-case surveillance alone. Meta-analysis suggests that seropositivity to H5N1 is uncommon in the general population but higher in exposed groups, consistent with occasional unrecognized infection [3]. During the H7N9 emergence in China, serologic studies in poultry workers and the general population found evidence of exposure gradients linked to live-bird markets and poultry handling [4]. For H9N2, multiple occupational studies in southern China documented elevated antibodies among poultry workers, supporting repeated low-level zoonotic transmission and the value of targeted serosurveillance in animal-exposed cohorts [5,6].

Swine-exposed populations similarly show elevated antibodies to variant and enzootic swine influenza viruses, highlighting agricultural interfaces as important sites of spillover risk. Prospective and cross-sectional studies in the United States and Europe found that farmers, veterinarians, and meat-processing workers had increased seroreactivity to swine-lineage H1 and H3 viruses compared with non-exposed controls [7,8]. Methodologically, the WHO seroepidemiologic investigation guideline and assay standardization work underscore that robust human exposure assessment depends on paired sera when possible, transparent seropositivity thresholds, adsorption or confirmatory microneutralization testing, and integration with detailed behavioral and occupational data [9,10].

Overall, seroepidemiology is most informative when embedded in One Health designs that link human antibody data to contemporaneous animal surveillance and viral genomics, allowing discrimination between sporadic exposure, sustained occupational risk, and early signals of adaptation at the animal–human interface.

subsections.section_title: Surveillance, Risk Assessment, and Predictive Frameworks
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Ranking and Predictive Modeling
subsections.content:
Risk ranking frameworks seek to prioritize the large diversity of influenza A viruses for intensified surveillance, laboratory characterization, and preparedness action. A widely used example is the CDC Influenza Risk Assessment Tool, which combines structured expert judgment across viral and population-level attributes to estimate both emergence potential and potential public-health impact, thereby supporting vaccine candidate selection and preparedness planning ref [203], ref [204]. Complementary semi-quantitative approaches have been developed for animal-origin influenza to rank strains by genetic, ecological, and epidemiological indicators of zoonotic concern ref [205].

Predictive modeling increasingly augments these expert-driven systems by linking sequence data to phenotypes associated with host range, receptor binding, transmission, and virulence. Comparative analyses have identified molecular signatures associated with adaptation of avian viruses to mammals, while machine-learning approaches have been used to infer zoonotic potential directly from viral protein sequences ref [206], ref [207], ref [208]. Phylogeographic and evolutionary models further help estimate spread, reassortment opportunity, and lineage persistence, which are relevant to spillover risk in rapidly changing poultry and wild-bird systems ref [209], ref [210].

Despite these advances, predictive performance remains constrained by ascertainment bias, uneven sampling across hosts and regions, limited negative datasets, and the context dependence of genotype-phenotype relationships. Recent work has therefore emphasized ensemble strategies that integrate genomic features, antigenic information, experimental data, and host-contact patterns, while explicitly representing uncertainty and validating predictions against prospective surveillance observations ref [204], ref [208], ref [211], ref [212].

subsections.section_title: Surveillance, Risk Assessment, and Predictive Frameworks
subsections.subsection_title: Data Gaps, Biases, and Surveillance Challenges
subsections.content:
Zoonotic risk estimates for influenza A are constrained by major sampling asymmetries across hosts, geographies, and production systems. Global sequence archives are dominated by outbreaks in commercial poultry and by countries with sustained diagnostic capacity, whereas endemic circulation in wild birds, backyard flocks, swine, and live-bird market networks is often undersampled, distorting inferred lineage diversity and spread ref [141], ref [213]. Passive, event-driven surveillance further overrepresents clinically obvious high-pathogenicity events and underdetects low-pathogenicity viruses with pandemic potential, a bias long recognized in avian influenza monitoring ref [214], ref [122].

Human-facing surveillance has parallel blind spots. Mild or subclinical zoonotic infections are easily missed without targeted serology and exposure-linked sampling, while heterogeneous assay platforms and seropositivity thresholds complicate comparisons across studies ref [215], ref [216]. Occupational cohorts provide valuable signal but are not representative of wider community exposure, and health-care-based case finding can preferentially detect severe disease. In swine, fragmented reporting and variable incentives for disclosure impede timely assessment of viruses at the animal-human interface, despite repeated evidence that agricultural fairs and production networks can seed reassortment and spillover risk ref [217], ref [218].

These biases propagate into predictive models: missing denominator data, inconsistent metadata, and delays in data sharing limit robust estimation of prevalence, host range, and genotype-phenotype associations. Reviews of zoonotic emergence preparedness have emphasized that surveillance remains weakly integrated across veterinary, public health, and environmental sectors, and that standardization of sampling frames, metadata, and open data practices is essential for risk ranking systems to be interpretable and actionable ref [219], ref [220].

subsections.section_title: Public Health Countermeasures, Prevention, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Animal and Human Vaccination Strategies
subsections.content:
Vaccination remains a central, but imperfect, countermeasure against zoonotic influenza A. In animal reservoirs, poultry vaccination can reduce clinical disease, viral shedding, and environmental contamination when matched vaccines are used within broader control programs; however, long-term field experience also shows that suboptimal coverage, antigenic mismatch, and weak surveillance can permit silent circulation and viral evolution ref [221], ref [222]. In China, large-scale H5/H7 vaccination in poultry was associated with marked declines in H7N9 detection in birds and human infections, illustrating the potential population-level benefit of coordinated veterinary immunization ref [223].

Human vaccination strategies must address both seasonal risk reduction and preparedness for novel strains. Seasonal influenza vaccination lowers opportunities for co-infection and may indirectly reduce reassortment risk in highly exposed groups, while prepandemic stockpiling of candidate vaccines against avian subtypes such as H5, H7, and H9 has shown variable but often improvable immunogenicity ref [224], ref [225]. Adjuvants are particularly important for dose sparing and breadth: MF59 and AS03 have enhanced responses to avian influenza vaccines, including cross-clade immunity in some H5N1 studies ref [226], ref [227].

Future vaccination strategies increasingly emphasize broadly protective platforms. Work on chimeric hemagglutinin, conserved-stalk immunogens, and mosaic designs seeks to overcome the narrow strain specificity that has limited both animal and human vaccines against rapidly evolving influenza A viruses ref [228], ref [229]. Even so, vaccine policy is likely to be most effective when linked to genomic surveillance, rapid seed-strain updating, targeted vaccination of high-risk occupational groups, and One Health evaluation of effects across animal and human populations ref [222], ref [230].

subsections.section_title: Public Health Countermeasures, Prevention, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Antiviral Therapies and Resistance Concerns
subsections.content:
Antiviral therapy remains a core countermeasure for zoonotic and pandemic-threat influenza A, particularly when strain-matched vaccines are unavailable or delayed. Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir and zanamivir can reduce viral replication and improve outcomes when given early, and observational data from hospitalized patients support benefit even in severe disease ref [231], ref [232]. However, clinical effectiveness is constrained by delayed presentation, limited access in some settings, and the rapid evolution of resistance under drug pressure.

Resistance concerns are most established for the adamantanes: single M2 substitutions, especially S31N, became globally fixed in many influenza A lineages, rendering amantadine and rimantadine largely obsolete for routine use ref [233], ref [234]. Neuraminidase inhibitor resistance also emerges through subtype-specific pathways, including H275Y in N1 viruses, which can retain substantial fitness and transmit efficiently ref [235], ref [236]. In avian-origin infections, prolonged viral replication in severely ill or immunocompromised hosts may further select resistant variants during therapy, underscoring the importance of virologic monitoring.

Newer agents expand the therapeutic landscape but also introduce fresh stewardship challenges. Baloxavir marboxil, a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor, produces rapid declines in viral load, yet PA I38 substitutions can reduce susceptibility and have already been detected after treatment ref [237], ref [238]. Favipiravir and polymerase-targeting combinations remain of interest for severe or resistant infections, with preclinical and early clinical data suggesting potential utility ref [239]. Future preparedness should therefore prioritize resistance surveillance across animal and human interfaces, stockpiling strategies that avoid overreliance on a single class, and evaluation of combination regimens to suppress resistance emergence ref [240].

subsections.section_title: Public Health Countermeasures, Prevention, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Biosecurity, Infection Control, and Market Interventions
subsections.content:
Biosecurity at the animal–human interface remains a primary barrier against zoonotic influenza A emergence. In poultry and swine systems, risk is amplified by high host density, species mixing, shared equipment, and movement of animals and workers across production nodes. Evidence from avian influenza control shows that strengthening farm-level hygiene, restricting movements, separating species, and rapidly removing infected flocks can reduce onward spread, although implementation is often uneven in smallholder and informal sectors ref [241], ref [242]. Reviews of highly pathogenic avian influenza epidemiology further emphasize that breaches along value chains—not only within farms—sustain transmission and create repeated opportunities for human exposure ref [243].

Live bird markets are a particularly important intervention point because they concentrate diverse avian hosts, virus-contaminated fomites, and intense human contact. Longitudinal studies in southern China showed that market rest days reduced virus isolation, and permanent closure of live poultry markets in affected cities was associated with marked declines in human H7N9 infection incidence ref [244], ref [80]. Environmental surveillance also demonstrates that markets can maintain substantial viral contamination, supporting interventions such as centralized slaughter, overnight depopulation, cleaning and disinfection, and species segregation ref [245], ref [246].

In healthcare and occupational settings, infection control must combine early case recognition, source control, personal protective equipment, and fit-for-purpose respiratory precautions for workers exposed to infected animals or suspected human cases. During outbreaks, these measures should be integrated with market regulation, compensation schemes that encourage reporting and culling, and risk communication that is feasible for traders and farmers. Modeling and field analyses suggest that interventions are most effective when coordinated across production, trade, and public health sectors rather than applied as isolated measures ref [247], ref [248].

Future priorities include evaluating compliance and cost-effectiveness of market restructuring, improving biosecurity in low-resource production systems, and embedding environmental and genomic surveillance into routine control programs to detect transmission hotspots before spillover escalates.

subsections.section_title: Public Health Countermeasures, Prevention, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Outbreak Preparedness and Pandemic Response Planning
subsections.content:
Outbreak preparedness for emerging zoonotic influenza A requires integrated surveillance, rapid risk assessment, and predefined decision frameworks that connect animal health signals to human public health action. Experience from H5N1 and H7N9 has shown that delays in case recognition, reporting, and characterization can amplify uncertainty and impede containment, whereas standardized assessment tools and pandemic phases can support earlier escalation of control measures and international coordination ref [249], ref [250], ref [251]. Scenario-based planning should therefore link genomic surveillance, animal outbreak intelligence, and clinical severity indicators to operational triggers for diagnostics, stockpile release, healthcare surge, and targeted non-pharmaceutical interventions ref [252], ref [253].

Preparedness plans must also incorporate flexible vaccine and antiviral deployment strategies. Analyses following the 2009 H1N1 pandemic emphasized that logistical constraints, manufacturing timelines, and prioritization decisions strongly shape vaccine impact, while mathematical modeling has shown that early antiviral treatment and prophylaxis can slow spread when implemented before widespread community transmission ref [254], ref [255], ref [256]. Because transmissibility and severity are uncertain early in emergence, pandemic plans should be explicitly adaptive, with provisions for real-time updating of severity assessments, supply-chain resilience, and equitable allocation of countermeasures across regions and risk groups ref [251], ref [254].

Finally, preparedness depends on routine intersectoral exercises, clear risk communication, and governance mechanisms that are functional before crises occur. Lessons from national and global reviews of pandemic preparedness underscore the need for sustained investment in laboratory capacity, hospital surge planning, and One Health coordination, rather than reactive planning after spillover events ref [257], ref [258]. For zoonotic influenza specifically, preparedness should include protocols for farm-to-community incident management, data sharing across veterinary and public health sectors, and pre-agreed policies for border measures, occupational protection, and continuity of essential services ref [252], ref [257].

subsections.section_title: Public Health Countermeasures, Prevention, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: One Health Governance and Policy Implications
subsections.content:
One Health governance for emerging influenza A requires institutional mechanisms that integrate animal, human, and environmental surveillance, risk assessment, and response rather than relying on ad hoc intersectoral coordination. Foundational frameworks argue that zoonotic risk is amplified when veterinary and public-health systems remain siloed, while integrated governance improves early warning and coordinated control across the farm–market–community interface ref [259], ref [260]. In influenza specifically, global analyses of avian and swine-origin emergence have shown that fragmented surveillance, delayed data sharing, and uneven laboratory capacity constrain timely detection of viruses with pandemic potential ref [261], ref [262].

Policy implications therefore include sustained investment in joint surveillance platforms, interoperable data standards, and transparent virus and sequence sharing under international norms. The revised WHO pandemic influenza preparedness guidance and the broader International Health Regulations architecture underscore that preparedness depends on linking animal outbreak intelligence to human-health decision making, while preserving incentives for countries to report events rapidly ref [258], ref [263]. Evidence from H5N1 governance debates further suggests that risk communication, benefit sharing, and biosafety oversight are not peripheral issues but central determinants of trust and compliance in One Health systems ref [264], ref [265].

A practical One Health policy agenda should also address upstream drivers of spillover, including poultry value-chain structure, live-bird market governance, and occupational exposure in intensive livestock production. Comparative work on emerging disease drivers and prevention has emphasized that governance must move beyond emergency response toward prevention-oriented regulation, compensation schemes, and cross-ministerial accountability that align agricultural productivity with health security goals ref [266], ref [267].

subsections.section_title: Public Health Countermeasures, Prevention, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging Research Priorities
subsections.content:
Emerging research priorities should move beyond reactive surveillance toward anticipatory risk assessment. Comparative analyses of avian influenza emergence have shown that host range shifts, reassortment, and mammalian-adaptive mutations can arise before sustained human transmission is recognized, underscoring the need for integrated genomic, phenotypic, and ecological surveillance across wildlife, poultry, swine, and exposed humans ref [268], ref [28], ref [269]. A related priority is improving fitness and transmissibility assessment for newly detected genotypes, including standardized experimental systems that better connect sequence variation with airborne transmission, tissue tropism, and pathogenicity in mammals ref [140], ref [270].

A second frontier is the development of broader and more durable countermeasures. Work on universal influenza vaccines highlights conserved HA stem, neuraminidase, and T-cell targets as promising routes, but correlates of cross-subtype protection remain incompletely defined ref [271]. In parallel, antiviral discovery should prioritize host-directed therapies and combinations that raise the barrier to resistance, especially given persistent concerns about reduced susceptibility to neuraminidase and polymerase inhibitors ref [272]. Better immunological studies in occupationally exposed and immunologically imprinted populations are also needed to understand how prior seasonal or zoonotic exposures shape susceptibility and vaccine performance ref [273].

Finally, preparedness research should incorporate social, environmental, and policy dimensions. One Health analyses indicate that land use change, poultry value chains, live-bird market dynamics, and farm biosecurity interact to structure spillover risk, yet these drivers are rarely modeled jointly with virological data ref [274]. Establishing interoperable data-sharing frameworks, evaluation metrics for interventions, and decision tools that link animal and human health intelligence to actionable thresholds should therefore be a major priority for future pandemic preparedness ref [275].
